Sensor fusion POC · 3 logged sessions · 11 on-periods

Predicting the stop, before the key is pressed

Girth and heart-rate velocity both roll over shortly before you press space. Here is where the detector fires in every on-period across all three sessions, and what the traces behind those numbers actually look like.

Does a shorter smoothing span help?

Yes — up to a point. The sensor sample rate is unchanged (girth ~8.9 Hz, HR ~2.7 Hz); what moves is the smoothing and derivative span, which sets how much lag the trigger carries. Shortening it makes the detector fire earlier and cuts late fires.

Below about 1 s it stops being a detector. The derivative becomes noise, the rollover trips immediately, and the fire time collapses onto the minimum-on-time floor — the same instant every episode regardless of what the signals do. The tracking column is the tell: it is the correlation between when the detector fires and how long the on-period actually lasted.

The 0.3 s row reaches zero late fires, but it is not a detector — its fire time has a standard deviation of 0.0 s. It stops two seconds after every resume, whatever the sensors are doing. A two-second timer would score identically.

The rule that works

Two changes over the 3 s version: a shorter span, and the rollover has to stay rolled over for a second before it counts. The hold is what removes the spurious early fires — girth velocity often dips once mid-rise and then climbs higher still.

on "S" (resume):  reset peak_g', peak_h', hold counters

every sample, causal — trailing 1.5 s mean, then
    g' = (g[t] − g[t−1.5s]) / 1.5        h' = (h[t] − h[t−1.5s]) / 1.5
    peak_g' = max(peak_g', g')           peak_h' = max(peak_h', h')

fire "space" when  t − t_resume ≥ 3 s  AND either channel satisfies
    peak ≥ 1 × MAD(derivative)   and   derivative ≤ 0.5 × peak
    continuously for 1.0 s

Thresholds are scaled to each channel's own MAD, so they carry across sessions with very different stimulation levels without retuning — which matters, because session 113316 had far less stimulation and a girth trace one-eighth the amplitude of the others.

The full context

All eleven on-periods, girth on the left and heart rate on the right, aligned so that zero is the moment you pressed space. The dotted line is the resume, the shaded band is the detector's lead.

What the traces show that the numbers don't

  • The two channels genuinely take turns. Six episodes fire on girth, five on HR. In 113316 girth spans forty counts and carries nothing — HR is the only reason those episodes fire at all. Dropping either channel loses episodes.
  • The rises are not smooth. Girth velocity is multi-peaked; the first rollover is often not the last. That is what the one-second hold is for, and it is where most of the remaining early error comes from.
  • The last episode of 113316 is a different animal. Both girth and HR are falling when space is pressed. The detector happens to land 1.7 s early, but not for the reason it does everywhere else. One episode, so not worth fitting to — worth watching for.
  • Short on-periods are the failure mode. Every large error, in both directions, sits on an on-period under 5 s or over 14 s. The middle band is where it is reliable.

Before trusting it

Eleven episodes, and the span, rollover fraction and hold were all chosen against them. The evaluation also resets the detector at each true mark, so it measures per-decision accuracy and excludes the error propagation that broke the free-running loop earlier.

To guarantee it never fires late you would need the minimum-on-time plus hold to come in under 3.7 s, which costs lead time on every long episode — or a hard on-time cap, which is a timer wearing a detector's clothes. Whether one late fire in eleven is acceptable is a call about what going over costs, not a question the data answers.
